cases.title: Regional imaging queue review
cases.dossier: The radiology board must decide this week whether to retain an AI queue rule at two hospitals. Routine examinations wait behind urgent reads; every examination eventually receives a radiologist report. The operations return shows shorter urgent reporting times, stable volume and no rise in recorded incidents. Staffing changed during the quarter, and a recruitment gap makes a return to the previous work allocation unattractive to the service manager. The quality dashboard compares triage categories with automated extraction of eventual radiology reports and describes high agreement. Its executive paragraph says: 'The completed quality evaluation found no clinically important abnormalities incorrectly assigned to the routine queue.' Patient representatives welcome faster urgent reports but ask whether routine patients wait longer. Finance reports that the pilot remains within its allocation. The clinical evaluation used an independent image reread; to preserve masking, clinical findings and operational assignments were held separately and reconciled after review. The committee pack contains only the executive paragraph, not the working returns. Existing clinical and information-system records can be retrieved, but no extra image reading can be commissioned before the meeting. Clinical staff can retain priority overrides if the service continues. The board wants a practical decision and defensible wording for its public summary.
cases.claim: The completed quality evaluation found no clinically important abnormalities incorrectly assigned to the routine queue.

documents.title: Finance return
documents.body: The quarter's expenditure is within the approved allocation. The saving is staff-time redeployment, not cash released. No expenditure field records clinical abnormalities or downstream patient harm.

documents.title: Service activity return
documents.body: Both sites sent consecutive eligible adult frontal chest examinations. Emergency resuscitation examinations were excluded from the queue policy. Every included image has a signed report. Reporting volume and urgent turnaround improved descriptively; staffing changed during the same quarter. A causal estimate of the AI's effect on waiting times is not available.

documents.title: Clinical sampling return
documents.body: Independent clinicians reread a random sample of examinations on which triage and automated extraction agreed, together with all disagreements. They saw images without either AI output or the queue assignment. The signed findings identify clinically important abnormalities requiring expedited assessment in examinations C17, C24, C38, C52, C61, C74 and C89. These identifiers refer to the same examinations as the operational reconciliation; no row is a duplicated patient encounter. Queue assignments are not included in this return because they were withheld from clinical reviewers. Follow-up on treatment and patient consequences was outside this reread's remit.

documents.title: Operations email
documents.body: For the next month, staff can maintain the existing human priority overrides and sample routine-queue records each week. The service cannot have every routine image independently reread before the meeting. A targeted clinical safety review can start next week. The safety lead owns escalation of any urgent discrepancy.

documents.title: Governance minutes
documents.body: The committee has not agreed a numerical acceptable clinical miss rate. It requires truthful public reporting and a plan for clinically significant discrepancies. It may continue a restricted monitored use or pause expansion while reviewing findings; either requires a named clinical owner.

documents.title: Information systems reconciliation
documents.body: The release log links the clinical-review identifiers to the original queue records. Examinations C17, C24, C38, C52, C61, C74 and C89 were assigned to the routine queue before radiologist reporting; this field is not a later discharge disposition. The clinical findings are held separately in the Clinical sampling return, not inferred from this queue field. The dashboard's comparison labels are automated report extractions. The operational dashboard was compiled before the independent returns were reconciled and was not republished afterward. The local incident register has no entry linking these examinations to a reported patient injury. The reconciliation contains no independently ascertained patient-outcome follow-up.

rubric.issue: AI agreement is not clinical reference truth; reconcile independent clinical findings with original queue assignments before assessing the no-misses statement.
rubric.action: Obtain clinical sampling and systems reconciliation; the seven shared identifiers connect important abnormalities to routine assignments. Correct the claim and review safeguards without asserting causal patient injury.
rubric.avoid: Treat automated labels as clinical truth, assume unrequested queue or clinical findings, or infer no abnormalities from stable incidents.

cases.title: Community follow-up scheduling decision
cases.dossier: A community service uses AI to allocate early follow-up after discharge. The committee is deciding whether to retain the current capped service for another quarter. Patients not prioritized retain standard access and a staffed escalation line. The operations dashboard reports fewer scheduling delays, stable clinical-indicator totals and favorable patient feedback. Routine follow-up staffing is funded. The service manager proposes retaining the existing allocation because changing schedules again would disrupt the next quarter's rota. The executive paragraph says: 'For the current eligible population, the pilot met the committee's agreed 30-day outcome criterion.' The outcome, comparison and acceptance rule were agreed before recruitment. The dashboard rounds its totals and does not reproduce the statistical analysis or the original committee agreement. Evaluation staff and the committee secretariat maintain separate records; neither has countersigned this executive paragraph. A patient representative asks about people who received no early call, while the finance lead wants reassurance that capped continuation requires no extra appointment capacity. Eligibility, sites and software remain unchanged. The board is not being asked to expand the service, but needs a defensible decision this week and instructions for next-quarter monitoring.
cases.claim: For the current eligible population, the pilot met the committee's agreed 30-day outcome criterion.

documents.title: Service experience note
documents.body: Patient interviews describe faster calls for many high-priority patients. Interviews are voluntary and do not estimate the clinical outcome. Scheduling time is a separate descriptive operational benefit.

documents.title: Workforce plan
documents.body: Named clinical and data leads will continue the evaluated service and monthly surveillance with existing funding. Active outcome ascertainment is funded for the next quarter. An unexpected serious event or material pathway change triggers clinical review.

documents.title: Committee agreement
documents.body: Before recruitment the committee adopted the following rule for the current eligible discharge population: the one-sided 95% upper uncertainty bound on additional 30-day clinically significant deterioration, relative to the randomized usual-care service, must lie below 1.0 percentage point. The same conclusion must hold in the prespecified conservative missing-outcome analysis. This locally negotiated tolerance is not a universal clinical standard. The agreement contains no pilot results and does not require superiority, zero risk or mortality improvement. Capped continuation is a separate policy decision informed by this result and service constraints.

documents.title: Budget return
documents.body: No extra staff are assumed in the proposed capped continuation. Additional expansion would require a separate business case. The present request concerns retention, not cash savings.

documents.title: Pilot analysis return
documents.body: The cluster-randomized evaluation included all eligible discharges, including standard-priority, failed-score and non-attending patients. Independent assessors blinded to allocation established 30-day clinically significant deterioration through a fixed clinical reference process, external-provider linkage and active contact. Ascertainment reached 99.9% in each group. The estimated excess versus randomized usual care was 0.1 percentage points; its one-sided 95% upper bound was 0.6 points. The prespecified conservative analysis of unresolved outcomes gave an upper bound of 0.7 points. Analysis incorporated clustering and baseline stratification. No material protocol departures were recorded. The locally agreed acceptance rule is held by the committee secretariat and is not reproduced in this statistical return. Mortality and longer-term outcomes were not assessed.

documents.title: Activity and eligibility extract
documents.body: Eligibility, model version and prioritization threshold are unchanged from the evaluated service. Every discharge enters the service register before AI scoring. Standard-priority and failed-score routes retain clinical access. No new population is being added in this decision.

rubric.issue: Reconcile the outcome analysis with the separately agreed decision criterion; verify coverage beyond early-call patients.
rubric.action: Obtain analysis and agreement; both upper bounds are below the local margin. Support proportionate capped continuation with monitoring, not universal safety.
rubric.avoid: Assume an unrequested margin or result, demand another trial despite adequate evidence, or invent an absent low-priority cohort after coverage is supplied.

cases.title: Teledermatology commissioning memo
cases.dossier: A district service uses AI to route adult skin-lesion referrals to urgent specialist assessment, routine assessment or return to primary care. Failed images go to a clinician. Commissioners are considering adding practices within the same district. Specialist waiting times fell and the pathway returned more referrals without a hospital visit. The report lists high diagnostic agreement in completed specialist episodes. The governance dashboard combines pathology results, hospital episode closure and complaints; it reports no new safety signal. The proposed statement is: 'The evaluation establishes that returning patients to primary care under this pathway does not increase delayed diagnosis of serious lesions.' The reporting period ended last month. The board has two weeks, a small nurse audit allocation and no agreed numerical tolerance for additional delayed diagnoses. The request concerns service commissioning, not advice about any individual lesion.
cases.claim: The evaluation establishes that returning patients to primary care under this pathway does not increase delayed diagnosis of serious lesions.

documents.title: Clinical information return
documents.body: Pathology and diagnostic agreement apply to patients assessed by hospital specialists. Return-to-primary-care records close administratively after the routing letter. No active outcome ascertainment was done in that route. A later hospital return is counted if linked, but external providers are not linked and linkage completeness has not been estimated. Absence of a complaint is not verified absence of a delayed diagnosis. Outcomes in patients never referred back remain unknown.

documents.title: Commissioning activity extract
documents.body: The referral register includes all received referrals, failed images and routing letters. It does not enumerate patients who never received a primary-care referral. The present claim concerns returned referrals, not all district residents. Specialist waiting-time summaries include only completed appointments.

documents.title: Nursing and data capacity note
documents.body: The nurse allocation can contact a probability sample of returned referrals and failed-score patients with primary-care support. Diagnostic assessment must use an agreed clinician-led pathway; universal biopsy is neither feasible nor an acceptable audit default. Obtaining mature delayed-diagnosis outcomes and external linkage will take months. No statistically justified audit size is yet available because event frequency, acceptable margin and follow-up completeness require work.

documents.title: Patient liaison summary
documents.body: Respondents appreciate shorter waits. Complaints include difficulty understanding return letters. Survey response is voluntary, and no clinical assessment accompanies the survey. Non-response cannot be read as a reassuring clinical outcome.

documents.title: Commercial and workforce return
documents.body: Current software and staff costs are within the pilot allocation. Adding practices is affordable only if fewer patients require hospital appointments. This assumption does not establish the clinical effect of those avoided appointments.

documents.title: Quality committee minutes
documents.body: No mandatory expansion date exists. Restricted continuation with clinical safeguards is available. The clinical lead must agree outcome definitions and escalation actions with commissioners before making an assurance about delayed diagnosis.

rubric.issue: Returned referrals lack ascertainment; hospital agreement/complaints do not identify delayed diagnoses in that route.
rubric.action: Request route-specific ascertainment and plan feasible independent follow-up; qualify expansion without asserting demonstrated harm.
rubric.avoid: More reviewed specialist records alone; universal biopsy; exact invented sample or proof of safety within two weeks.

cases.title: Teledermatology service retention memo
cases.dossier: The district board is deciding whether to retain its capped adult teledermatology service, with the same practices, model and clinical override arrangements. Its prespecified independent evaluation sampled every routing stratum from the full referral register, including return-to-primary-care and failed-score routes, with known sampling weights. Clinicians blinded to the AI result adjudicated the agreed clinically significant delayed-diagnosis endpoint after mature follow-up. Primary-care contact and outside-provider records supplemented hospital linkage. Ascertainment was 99%; a conservative missing-outcome sensitivity analysis retained the conclusion. The risk difference versus the concurrent randomized usual-care pathway was 0.1 percentage points; the prespecified one-sided 95% upper bound was 0.4 points, below the board's previously agreed 0.8-point margin. The weighting and clustered design were included in that interval. The report's claim is: 'The evaluated service met the board's local delayed-diagnosis criterion for the included population and follow-up period.' Populations excluded from evaluation remain outside this service, with clinician pathways unchanged. The board does not claim zero risk, benefit for excluded populations or long-term cancer survival. Current monitoring and staffing are funded.
cases.claim: The evaluated service met the board's local delayed-diagnosis criterion for the included population and follow-up period.

documents.title: Evaluation sign-off
documents.body: Independent clinical and statistical reviewers confirm the methods and values in the committee dossier. The protocol and margin were signed before recruitment; no material departures were found. Known weights and clustering were included. The report supports its stated bounded criterion. The local margin is a committee choice, not a universal medical standard.

documents.title: Implementation register
documents.body: Model, threshold, sites and eligible population are unchanged. Excluded patients retain clinician assessment. A model or population change requires a new applicability review before use.

documents.title: Patient service summary
documents.body: Patient surveys are favorable but are not part of the clinical safety endpoint. Neither survey satisfaction nor reduced appointments alone supports clinical safety; the independent evaluation does that for its stated scope.

documents.title: Workforce and surveillance plan
documents.body: A named safety lead owns continuing outcome linkage, periodic independently assessed samples and clinical escalation. Existing funding covers this capped service. New serious signals trigger a clinical review; expansion is a separate decision.

documents.title: Finance report
documents.body: The capped service is within its current allocation. No additional saving or new population is assumed. Funding beyond the current contract will be reviewed separately.

documents.title: Clinical governance minutes
documents.body: The committee accepts the prespecified local margin for this decision. It requires continued surveillance rather than proof that no adverse outcome can ever occur. Broader claims are not being requested.

rubric.issue: Adequate ascertainment and precision support a narrow local criterion already in the dossier.
rubric.action: Accept the criterion and proportionate retention with funded safeguards; no extra document is required.
rubric.avoid: Invent missing returned patients, demand an arbitrary new RCT or equate support with zero risk.

cases.title: Diabetes eye-screening access review
cases.dossier: A diabetes clinic introduced point-of-care AI retinal screening. All patients due for screening appear in its invitation register. Attendance and image completion increased, and the quarterly dashboard reports that nearly all positive results generated a referral. Ungradable images are referred for clinical assessment. The board paper calls the screening gap closed and proposes: 'The service has demonstrated improved completion of indicated specialist care within six months.' Enrollment began eight weeks ago, and participants continue to enter. A liaison team is reconciling specialist records across providers. The next budget decision is in ten days. The board may fund screening and navigation separately, and does not require the claim of downstream benefit to fund screening access. There is no comparison-group report in the dossier.
cases.claim: The service has demonstrated improved completion of indicated specialist care within six months.

documents.title: Specialist liaison return
documents.body: The six-month follow-through return is not yet available: the oldest participants have eight weeks of follow-up. The system records referrals sent, not confirmed completed specialist care. Cross-provider attendance linkage is being negotiated; current unmatched entries are unknown, not confirmed non-attendance. No comparator for six-month care completion has been assembled. A complete six-month outcome analysis cannot exist by the decision in ten days.

documents.title: Screening register
documents.body: All eligible clinic patients due for screening are recorded before the offer, including non-attenders, ungradable images and positives. Screening completion is measured reliably within this clinic. Increased screening is a real observed access metric; it is distinct from attending a specialist or receiving indicated treatment.

documents.title: Navigation staffing note
documents.body: One navigator can reconcile existing appointments, contact people with unresolved referrals and arrange accessible follow-up. This is a care intervention as well as ascertainment; future outcome estimates must describe that intervention. It cannot make six months elapse within ten days.

documents.title: Technical image quality appendix
documents.body: A specialist overreads the screening images under the pilot's quality process. This supports image-result review; it does not establish whether patients later attended or completed care. Ungradable images follow the same clinical referral route.

documents.title: Budget options
documents.body: The board can retain capped screening and fund navigation without making an effectiveness claim about specialist completion. The reserve does not cover a new region-wide records platform this month.

documents.title: Patient experience interviews
documents.body: Patients value screening during their usual clinic visit. Several describe transport and work barriers to separate appointments. Interviews are not representative clinical outcome ascertainment and do not identify the attendance status of uncontacted patients.

rubric.issue: Screening/referral is not completed specialist care; follow-up is immature and comparison absent.
rubric.action: Retain narrower access benefit, plan linkage/navigation and mature follow-up; acknowledge impossibility before this deadline.
rubric.avoid: Treat unmatched as nonattendance, require withdrawing useful screening, or promise mature six-month proof in ten days.

cases.title: Integrated retinal pathway contract review
cases.dossier: An integrated diabetes service proposes renewing an AI screening plus referral contract. Screening completion is substantially higher than under the previous service. The pilot followed participants for six months, and a clinical audit reconciled care at internal and external providers. The board's exact claim is: 'The evaluated pathway met our pre-agreed criterion that at least 80% of patients needing specialist assessment complete it within six months.' This is a local contract target, not a universal clinical threshold. The executive summary says 'follow-through reviewed' without reporting its denominator or result; it emphasizes the screening improvement. The responsible clinical auditor can supply the signed reconciliation. The board can retain screening while changing navigation or referral capacity. Renewal does not require claiming that better screening caused better visual outcomes.
cases.claim: The evaluated pathway met our pre-agreed criterion that at least 80% of patients needing specialist assessment complete it within six months.

documents.title: Signed clinical reconciliation
documents.body: Of 100 patients requiring specialist assessment, 62 completed it within six months, 30 were confirmed not to have attended and eight remained unresolved after external-provider reconciliation and contact attempts. Even if all eight unresolved patients had completed assessment, the fraction would be 70%, below the pre-agreed 80% criterion. The denominator includes AI positives and ungradable images requiring assessment. Classification was adjudicated independently of the AI dashboard. Follow-up is mature for all 100. The pathway therefore did not meet the stated criterion. The audit does not show that AI caused the failure or that vision outcomes worsened.

documents.title: Clinic activity register
documents.body: Screening completion rose from 56% to 90% of eligible patients across successive service periods. These are reliable descriptive clinic proportions, not a randomized causal comparison. The service register includes non-attenders and failed images.

documents.title: Referral operations note
documents.body: Navigation calls and protected specialist appointments can be funded by shifting part of the proposed expansion budget. The clinical lead can prioritize urgent unresolved referrals immediately. No full rollout is needed to implement these improvements.

documents.title: Technical quality report
documents.body: Image overreading found acceptable agreement for the local screening protocol. This does not establish care completion. The audit's care outcomes are held in the Signed clinical reconciliation.

documents.title: Commissioning minutes
documents.body: The 80% target was approved before the pilot and concerns actual six-month assessment completion, not referrals sent. The board can recognize the screening gain while acknowledging that the completion criterion was not met.

documents.title: Patient communication review
documents.body: Letters meet the accessibility standard but patients report scheduling and travel barriers. These findings suggest changes to test; they do not alone establish which specific change would improve attendance.

rubric.issue: The complete care audit, not the screening rate, decides the local completion criterion.
rubric.action: Obtain reconciliation, acknowledge criterion failure even under best-case missing outcomes, preserve screening benefit and repair follow-through.
rubric.avoid: Assume all unresolved missed care, assert AI caused failure, or endorse criterion on screening success alone.

cases.title: Primary-care metabolic testing allocation
cases.dossier: A network uses an EHR risk score to prioritize metabolic testing appointments. Its payer report shows lower testing costs and fewer newly coded diagnoses among people assigned lower priority. The report describes this as better allocation of prevention resources. Some adults have long local records; others joined recently or have care elsewhere. Performance was checked against diagnoses appearing in the EHR over the following year. The board claim is: 'The reduced rate of newly coded diagnoses in lower-priority patients demonstrates that the pathway prevented incident disease.' It wants to continue the present allocation while reducing routine appointments. The report contains no independently measured baseline disease assessment. Clinicians retain the ability to order tests, and the committee has not agreed a numerical tolerance for undetected disease.
cases.claim: The reduced rate of newly coded diagnoses in lower-priority patients demonstrates that the pathway prevented incident disease.

documents.title: Model and data specification
documents.body: The model predicts a future coded diagnosis, not directly measured disease onset. Newly enrolled patients and those without recent tests frequently have no code. The training target counts diagnoses made during routine care; care intensity affects whether labels appear. No baseline independent assessment separates previously undetected disease from new onset. Fewer codes could reflect fewer opportunities to detect disease and cannot establish prevention.

documents.title: Clinical audit extract
documents.body: The performance audit sampled patients who later received a metabolic test. Low-priority untested patients did not receive independent assessment. External records are incomplete and capture of outside diagnoses is unknown. The audited agreement is therefore conditional on being tested; the frequency of undetected disease in the untested route remains unknown.

documents.title: Practice operations note
documents.body: Practices can offer a consented probability sample an appropriate clinician-led assessment, including low-priority patients and people with sparse histories. This can assess current undetected disease but cannot retrospectively establish exact onset or prove the policy prevented disease. Estimating prevention would require a suitable comparison and time-aligned baseline/follow-up. The local harm tolerance remains a committee decision.

documents.title: Payer expenditure return
documents.body: Costs and testing volume fell in the reported period. This is measured utilization, not a health-need measure. Contracts pay for tests delivered; diagnoses outside the network may not produce local claims.

documents.title: Population registration note
documents.body: The registration list includes established, newly enrolled and intermittently attending adults. Sparse histories indicate incomplete observation, not absence of disease. The population denominator can be constructed without restricting to people who had tests.

documents.title: Patient access interviews
documents.body: Patients describe mixed experiences: fewer appointments for some, concern about obtaining tests for others. These interviews neither verify undetected disease nor establish causal prevention benefits.

rubric.issue: Codes reflect detection/care intensity, not onset or prevention; untested and sparse-history patients lack ascertainment.
rubric.action: Separate existing undetected disease from incidence; representative clinical assessment for the former, suitable longitudinal comparison for prevention.
rubric.avoid: Call lower utilization improved health or claim a cross-sectional audit proves prevention; interpret sparse histories as healthy.

cases.title: Metabolic case-finding audit review
cases.dossier: A network trial of AI-prioritized metabolic testing is reviewing a small independently assessed sample. Sampling began from all eligible registered adults, including untested people and sparse-history patients; everyone selected received the same blinded clinician-led reference assessment. Follow-up and reference assessment are complete. The network's board claim is: 'This audit establishes that the prevalence of clinically actionable undetected disease among patients assigned lower priority is below our pre-agreed 2% tolerance.' The dashboard reports no events in the completed lower-priority sample. The short executive note does not state its size or interval. The board is deciding whether to reduce the retained usual-care testing capacity. The statistical appendix and operations note can be requested. The 2% tolerance is a local decision, not an asserted medical standard.
cases.claim: This audit establishes that the prevalence of clinically actionable undetected disease among patients assigned lower priority is below our pre-agreed 2% tolerance.

documents.title: Statistical appendix
documents.body: There were zero clinically actionable cases in 30 randomly selected lower-priority adults. All selected adults received independent blinded reference assessment. The prespecified one-sided exact 95% upper bound is 9.50%, well above the board's 2% tolerance. The sample is representative but too small for the stated assurance. No subgroup was systematically omitted and outcome data are complete. Zero observed cases is not proof that the underlying prevalence exceeds 2%, either.

documents.title: Audit methods sign-off
documents.body: The sampling register covered all eligible adults before testing decisions. The random lower-priority sample included sparse histories and untested patients. All selected patients completed the same blinded reference assessment. This is a prevalence audit at the assessment date, not an incidence or prevention study.

documents.title: Workforce planning note
documents.body: The remaining allocation supports 20 additional independent assessments before the committee meets. Even another 20 without an event would leave the one-sided exact 95% upper bound about 5.82%, still above 2%. A later larger audit can be planned, but the present budget cannot meet the proposed assurance before this decision. Existing usual-care testing capacity can be retained meanwhile.

documents.title: Committee tolerance record
documents.body: The 2% threshold and one-sided 95% uncertainty rule were agreed before recruitment. The committee requires the uncertainty bound, not only the point estimate, to lie below the tolerance before reducing usual-care testing capacity.

documents.title: Finance ledger
documents.body: The proposed saving assumes reduced routine testing capacity. Retention for another quarter is financially possible. Audit assessments incur clinical staffing costs; the current allocation is described in the Workforce planning note.

documents.title: Practice experience summary
documents.body: Practices report that the prioritization interface is usable. Satisfaction and throughput do not increase statistical precision of the audit. No disease-incidence claim is included in the board request.

rubric.issue: Relevant patients are observed; uncertainty rather than missing ascertainment prevents assurance.
rubric.action: Use supplied interval, recognize current capacity cannot settle threshold, retain capacity or explicitly conditional decision; plan a justified larger audit later.
rubric.avoid: Invent missing patients, call zero events proof of adequacy, say prevalence is demonstrated above tolerance, or promise sufficient precision from 20 more.
